name: HTTP 402 Payment Required repurposed for pay-per-crawl AI-content monetization -- Cloudflare's 'AI Crawl Control' / 'Pay per crawl' product (launched beta July 2025, GA per later 2026 sources) and the adjacent open x402 protocol (Coinbase-backed, x402 Foundation) for onchain stablecoin micropayments, both built on the previously-dormant HTTP 402 status code and Web Bot Auth (Ed25519 HTTP Message Signatures) for crawler authentication.
kind: A commercial product/edge-enforcement service (Cloudflare Pay per crawl / AI Crawl Control) plus an emerging open payment protocol (x402), layered on top of a revived, decades-old but historically unused HTTP status code (402 Payment Required). Not a standard in the IETF sense (no RFC governs this specific reuse, though HTTP 402 itself is defined in RFC 9110 as reserved for future use), but rapidly becoming a de facto convention given Cloudflare's edge-network scale.
maturity: Launched as closed beta July 2025 (per Cloudflare's own changelog: 2025-07-01 pay-per-crawl, 2025-08-27 AI Crawl Control launch), reaching apparent general availability by 2026 sources ('AI Crawl Control GA: Publisher Economics Reset 2026'). Real, large-scale production deployment: Cloudflare customers are reported sending over 1 BILLION HTTP 402 responses to AI crawlers PER DAY through this system as of 2026 -- this is not a research prototype, it is live infrastructure at web-scale. The complementary x402 protocol (Coinbase/x402 Foundation) is newer and being integrated into Cloudflare Workers as a 'Monetization Gateway' with an open waitlist announced July 2026.
license: Cloudflare's Pay per crawl is a commercial product (Cloudflare acts as 'Merchant of Record' for transactions); x402 is described as an 'open protocol/standard' though its governance and licensing terms were not independently confirmed in this pass. Not a licensing concern for this project unless it becomes either a payer (an AI agent paying for access) or a payee (monetizing its own content) under this system.
keeps_and_discards: Not an extractor. The mechanism KEEPS the existing HTTP request/response cycle unchanged in shape (still a GET request, still a status code response) while DISCARDING the assumption that a 402 response is unused/meaningless -- it repurposes RFC 9110's long-reserved-but-unspecified 402 status into a concrete, machine-actionable 'pay this amount and retry' signal. It DISCARDS card-based payment rails entirely in favor of either Cloudflare's own billing-aggregation model (crawler pays Cloudflare, Cloudflare pays the publisher) or, in the x402 variant, real-time onchain stablecoin settlement -- both chosen specifically because traditional card-processing fees make sub-cent/few-cent micropayments economically unviable.
structure_preserved: Not applicable in the content-structure sense -- this is a transport/authorization-layer mechanism, not a content-representation concern.
interactive_elements: Not directly applicable to page content, though conceptually parallel: the entire mechanism is itself a machine-to-machine 'interactive' negotiation (request, 402-with-price, signed-retry-with-payment, 200-with-charge-confirmation) -- a fully automated interaction flow rather than a human-facing one, useful context for how this project might reason about designing analogous machine-negotiated protocols if ever relevant.
layout_awareness: Not applicable -- purely an HTTP-header-level mechanism, no layout/geometry involvement.
javascript_required: No -- the flow operates entirely at the HTTP request/response header level (a crawler's own client library constructs signed requests and reads price headers); no script execution is needed to participate, consistent with this being designed for headless/API-style AI crawler clients, not browser-rendering agents specifically (though nothing prevents a browser-based agent from also implementing the same header flow).
evaluation_method: Not a benchmark in the academic sense -- evidence comes from Cloudflare's own product documentation/blog (vendor-produced) plus independent journalism/analyst coverage of adoption statistics (see corpus_size_and_origins). No controlled experiment measuring the mechanism's own correctness/robustness was found in available sources -- this item's evidence base is PRODUCTION DEPLOYMENT DATA, not a research evaluation.
corpus_size_and_origins: Adoption figure from an independent 2026 survey: 'about 10.13% of nearly 300,000 domains surveyed' had adopted pay-per-crawl-style monetization, described as 'fairly uniform across traffic tiers' (i.e. not concentrated only among the largest sites, though see the SMB-implementation-capacity caveat below). Named early adopters (large publishers, not independently verified beyond the search-summary source): Condé Nast, Time, the Associated Press, BuzzFeed, Reddit, Pinterest, Stack Overflow. Scale of live traffic: 'more than one billion HTTP 402 Payment Required responses... per day' across Cloudflare's AI Crawl Control customer base. Crawler-traffic composition shift: Cloudflare's own June 2026 breakdown reports 52% of crawler requests now fall in the 'AI training' bucket, up sharply from 22% in spring 2025 -- a fast-moving, vendor-reported trend figure (should be read as Cloudflare's own traffic classification, not an independently audited figure).
reported_precision_recall: Not a precision/recall-style metric -- the relevant reported figures are adoption percentage (10.13% of ~300,000 domains), revenue potential (high-traffic sites reportedly able to earn $50,000-$200,000/month from AI crawler fees, a WIDE and unverified range from a single search-summary source), and cost-impact projections (if top-10K publishers broadly adopt fees, training-data acquisition costs for AI developers could 'surge 30-60%,' again an unverified projective estimate rather than a measured outcome). SMB implementation gap: 'only 22% of SMB sites have resources to implement fee structures' -- a capacity/equity finding structurally similar to the EDPB compliance-burden-asymmetry finding in item 11 (large operators absorb new overhead more easily than small ones).
independent_oracle: Weak for this item specifically -- most of the adoption/revenue figures found trace back to a mix of Cloudflare's own reporting (traffic composition, 1B/day 402 responses) and secondary analyst/blog commentary (adoption percentage, revenue ranges) rather than a peer-reviewed or independently-audited dataset; treat all quantitative figures in this item as DIRECTIONALLY informative but not independently verified to research-grade rigor.
evidence_independence: Mixed and should be read carefully: Cloudflare is both the PRODUCT VENDOR and a primary source of the traffic-volume/composition statistics cited here (1B/day, 52%-training-traffic), meaning those specific figures are vendor-self-reported. The adoption-percentage figure (10.13% of ~300k domains) and the named-publisher-adopter list appear to come from independent survey/analyst sources, giving this item a partially-independent but not fully-independent evidence base overall.
page_archetype_coverage: Not applicable -- pricing in the base mechanism is set 'per zone' (whole-site or whole-subdomain in Cloudflare's terminology), not per page-archetype; no evidence found of per-content-type differential pricing (e.g. charging more for high-value structured data than for boilerplate pages) in the current implementation, though this is architecturally possible via path-scoped rules and simply not confirmed as deployed.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Not addressed -- no language/locale dimension found in available sources for this mechanism.
leaks_outward: Not a data-leakage concern in the usual sense -- the mechanism is designed to be transparent/declarative (both sides know the price and the transaction occurred); the one privacy-adjacent consideration is that x402's ONCHAIN stablecoin settlement makes payment transactions publicly visible on whatever blockchain is used, a genuinely different privacy posture from a private card transaction or Cloudflare's own aggregated-billing model, not discussed as a tradeoff in available sources.
mechanism_detectability: The AUTHENTICATION side of this mechanism is explicitly built to be non-spoofable-by-design via Web Bot Auth: crawlers generate Ed25519 keypairs, publish JWK-formatted public keys at a hosted 'key directory' URL, register that URL plus their user-agent string with Cloudflare, and sign EVERY request using the HTTP Message Signatures standard -- meaning a crawler identity under this system is cryptographically verifiable, not just a spoofable User-Agent string. This is directly relevant to this project's own mechanism_detectability concerns in the MIRROR sense: if this project's own sensor ever needed to identify itself as a legitimate, well-behaved crawler to a site using this system, it would need to implement the SAME signed-request protocol (signature-agent / signature-input / signature headers) rather than relying on an easily-spoofed identity string, and conversely, a site cannot use THIS mechanism to detect a browser-based sensor that is not making its OWN independent HTTP requests but instead reading a live rendered page (a structurally different capture method this payment protocol does not contemplate at all).
countermeasures: The entire mechanism IS a countermeasure (against uncompensated bulk scraping), whose own effectiveness at directing/limiting crawler behavior was not independently measured in available sources beyond the adoption-rate figures; a genuinely open question this research pass could not resolve is what happens to a crawler that IGNORES the 402 response and simply does not retry -- does that crawler's request simply fail (does the origin never receive the content, i.e. is this actually enforced at the edge before origin) or is enforcement bypassable? The one confirmed relevant detail: 'if you block an AI crawler from a zone via either of Cloudflare's WAF or Bot Management products, those products' rulesets will OVERRIDE pay per crawl's charge feature' -- i.e. an explicit WAF block takes precedence over the pay-to-access flow, meaning pay-per-crawl is a MIDDLE OPTION between fully open and fully blocked, not itself the strongest enforcement layer available.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not a fidelity-hardening-cost question in the usual sense of this research set (this mechanism does not degrade content fidelity, it gates ACCESS); the closest analogue is the economic cost distribution finding: SMB-scale sites face a real implementation-capacity gap (only 22% report having resources to set up fee structures) versus large publishers who can and do (the named adopter list skews toward major media/tech brands), meaning the mechanism's PRACTICAL availability is itself scale-dependent even though the underlying protocol is open to any site.
gate_state_at_capture: Directly and centrally relevant: a 402 response IS a distinct, well-defined GATE STATE this project's own capture pipeline could and should record separately from a generic 403/401 block or a CAPTCHA challenge (per the taxonomy already established in item 12's HasData findings, where 402 was measured as 10.9% of declared-ban enforcement responses) -- this project's gate_state_at_capture field should treat 'payment required, price quoted' as its OWN distinct category, since it carries additional structured information (the quoted price itself) beyond a simple binary blocked/allowed signal.
determinism: The PROTOCOL flow itself (request -> 402-with-price -> signed-retry-with-payment -> 200-with-charge-confirmation) is deterministic given fixed pricing configuration, but the PRICE itself is a live, site-operator-configurable value that can change between requests -- meaning a captured 'price at time T' is not guaranteed valid at time T+1, a real-time-pricing property this project would need to handle if it ever participated in this system (price must be re-checked per request, not cached long-term, unlike the 24-hour robots.txt caching window noted in item 12).
determinism_across_versions: Not addressed in available sources -- x402 and Cloudflare's own implementation are both actively evolving (x402's Monetization Gateway only reached open-waitlist stage in July 2026 per sources found), so header names/semantics should be expected to continue changing.
reproducibility: The underlying protocol (once documented) is reproducible by any client implementing the correct signed-header flow; the ECONOMIC outcomes (adoption rate, revenue figures) are point-in-time measurements subject to rapid change given how new and fast-growing this space is (traffic composition alone shifted from 22% to 52% AI-training share in roughly one year per Cloudflare's own reported figures).
failure_modes: Not extensively documented as a technical failure taxonomy in available sources (unlike item 12's HasData study, no equivalent rigorous live-measurement study of 402/pay-per-crawl ENFORCEMENT reliability was found) -- this is a genuine evidence gap for this item, flagged in uncertain below. The one architecturally notable failure-adjacent finding: WAF/Bot-Management rules OVERRIDE the pay-per-crawl charge feature, meaning a site could inconsistently apply blocking vs. charging depending on which product/ruleset a given request trips first, a source of potential non-obvious behavior for any crawler trying to reason about a site's actual access policy from outside.
failure_visibility: The mechanism is DESIGNED to be loud by construction -- a 402 response with an explicit price is about as unambiguous a machine-readable signal as this research set has surfaced (contrast with item 12's finding that robots.txt bans are silently unenforced 39.5% of the time): if a crawler receives 402, it KNOWS exactly why and exactly what would need to happen to proceed, no ambiguity about whether the block is real or accidental.
scale_limits: The 1-billion-per-day 402-response figure demonstrates the mechanism operates at genuine internet scale already; no evidence of the mechanism itself becoming a scale-limiting bottleneck was found (Cloudflare's edge-network architecture is specifically designed to reject unpaid requests AT THE EDGE before they ever reach origin infrastructure -- 'only paid, authenticated traffic reaches origin; freeloaders die at the edge' -- meaning the mechanism is explicitly an origin-server LOAD-REDUCTION technique as much as a monetization one).
delta_cost_model: Not applicable in this project's O(delta) ingest sense -- this is a per-request access-control/billing mechanism, not an incremental-content-update concept; each request is priced and settled independently.
reanchoring_stability: Not applicable -- no DOM-element-identity concept in this mechanism.
adversarial_exposure: Not a content-injection concern; the closest adjacent risk is economic/gaming-oriented and not deeply explored in available sources: could a malicious actor spoof a LOW-value crawler-max-price to underpay, or exploit the proactive-price-declaration flow to probe pricing without ever completing payment? The Ed25519-signed-request design specifically defeats IDENTITY spoofing, but whether it also defeats PRICE-NEGOTIATION gaming (e.g. repeated proactive low-ball offers) was not addressed in available sources.
provenance_carrying: Directly relevant in one specific way: a successful transaction under this system carries an explicit `crawler-charged` confirmation header, which functions as a verifiable PROOF-OF-LAWFUL-ACCESS provenance marker this project could record per capture (distinct from, and complementary to, the declared-vs-enforced gate-state provenance discussed in item 12) -- 'this content was captured after a confirmed, priced, paid transaction' is a strong, auditable provenance claim if this project ever operates as a paying crawler under such a system.
roundtrip_safety: Not applicable -- no serialize/reparse concept in this mechanism.
token_budget_and_ordering: Not applicable directly, though economically adjacent: if this project's own downstream consumers (an SLM-facing agent) had to factor PER-REQUEST MONETARY COST into what content to retrieve, that would introduce an entirely new axis of prioritization beyond token budget -- a genuinely novel consideration this research set has not otherwise surfaced, worth flagging as a forward-looking design question even though no source directly addresses it for this project's specific architecture.
representation_cost: Not applicable in the token-efficiency sense; the closest analogue is monetary cost-per-fetch, an entirely different resource axis than token/representation cost.
what_could_be_adopted: One clear mechanism, one clear open question, one caution. ADOPTABLE: treat HTTP 402 as its own distinct, structured gate-state category in this project's own capture-metadata schema (per gate_state_at_capture above) -- recording not just 'gated: yes/no' but the QUOTED PRICE when a 402 is encountered, since that price is itself meaningful structured data (a site's own valuation signal for its content) worth preserving even if this project never actually pays it. OPEN QUESTION THIS PROJECT SHOULD RESOLVE EXPLICITLY, NOT DEFAULT INTO: whether this project's own capture activity should ever attempt to PAY for gated content under this system -- doing so would require implementing the full Web-Bot-Auth signed-request flow and taking on a genuine financial-transaction dimension this research pass takes no position on, but which the project's own governance posture should decide deliberately rather than accidentally (e.g. by a sensor that silently retries with a max-price header without an explicit human decision to enable that). CAUTION: given the near-total absence of an independent enforcement-reliability study for 402/pay-per-crawl (unlike item 12's rigorous robots.txt enforcement measurement), this project should NOT assume a 402 response is more reliably enforced than a robots.txt Disallow just because it looks more concrete -- that assumption is currently UNVERIFIED by any source found in this research pass.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- purely a transport/access-control-layer mechanism, no page-region classification involved. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- entirely orthogonal to rendered layout. o_delta: NOT APPLICABLE -- no incremental-update concept; each request/payment cycle is independent. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, WITH AN IMPORTANT CAVEAT -- if this project ever implements the payment flow, it must be tested against a REAL payment/settlement path (real Cloudflare sandbox or real x402 testnet, not a stubbed 200-response mock), consistent with the project's own no-mocks discipline; but given the genuine financial-transaction risk involved, this is exactly the kind of feature that should require EXPLICIT, deliberate opt-in rather than being silently exercised by an automated pipeline (an important distinction from most other no-mocks-compliant features in this research set, which carry no direct monetary risk). closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NOT APPLICABLE -- orthogonal to shadow-DOM capture policy. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is at the RECORDING/METADATA level (treat 402+price as a first-class gate-state signal), but the PAYMENT-PARTICIPATION question is a genuine, unresolved governance decision this project should make deliberately rather than default into, and the enforcement-reliability evidence base for this specific mechanism is thinner than for robots.txt (item 12), so any reliability claim about it should stay appropriately hedged.
governance_signal_handling: Directly complementary to item 12: HTTP 402 is best understood as the ENFORCEMENT/MONETIZATION layer sitting alongside the DECLARATIVE-PREFERENCE layer (robots.txt/Content Signals/AIPREF) -- no explicit integration between the two was confirmed in available sources (Cloudflare's own pay-per-crawl documentation did not mention robots.txt/Content-Signals interaction directly), meaning a site could in principle have inconsistent or unlinked declared-preference and payment-gate configurations, a real integration gap this project should not assume is resolved.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Not directly addressed in available sources for the payment mechanism itself; the x402 onchain-settlement variant introduces a genuinely NEW consideration not present in the rest of this research set -- a blockchain-recorded payment transaction is a different kind of persistent, public record than any other artifact discussed here, and if this project ever became a payer under that specific variant, the implications for its own operational privacy (a permanent, public, linkable transaction trail of what it accessed and when) would need dedicated review beyond what any source in this pass addresses.
uncertain: No independently-measured enforcement-reliability study (analogous to item 12's HasData paired-request methodology) for HTTP 402/pay-per-crawl was found -- whether declared 402 gates are actually, reliably enforced at the rate they claim to be is UNVERIFIED by any source in this research pass

Exact revenue figures ($50,000-$200,000/month for high-traffic sites) and cost-impact projections (30-60% training-data cost surge) both trace to single, unverified secondary sources and should be treated as rough industry estimates, not measured outcomes
Whether/how x402's onchain settlement and Cloudflare's own aggregated-billing model will converge, compete, or coexist long-term was not confirmed

The named early-adopter publisher list (Conde Nast, Time, AP, BuzzFeed, Reddit, Pinterest, Stack Overflow) was not independently cross-verified beyond the single search-summary source that reported it
Whether path-scoped (as opposed to whole-zone) differential pricing is actually deployed/used in practice, versus only architecturally possible, was not confirmed
